Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette: Mai’s life shifted after the November incident three years ago. She was forty-five then, sitting across from her partner at their dining table when he suddenly stood and lunged. She backed into the entryway, where a heavy glass doorstop had been left near the hallway mirror. He shoved her against the wall; the glass cracked, and a chef’s knife, resting on the counter behind him, slid to the floor. She remembers the exact angle of the blade on the linoleum, the way the overhead light caught its edge, and the rigid set of his shoulders. He had driven her back until the hallway mirror caught their reflection, forcing her to watch the scene unfold in glass while his face twisted into a posture she no longer recognized. There was no warning, no gradual escalation. Just the sudden violence and the chilling proximity of an object that could have ended her. In the weeks that followed, Mai found herself living inside a constant state of alert. Her body would tense at the sound of a closing door before her mind registered what the sound meant. She noticed every potentially dangerous object in a room: shears in desk drawers, heavy books, the weight of a metal lamp. She kept checking mirrors in hallways and bathrooms, watching her own reflection as if it might signal whether she was still safe. When she tried to recount the November event, her recollections refused to flow. Instead, she experienced it as disconnected snapshots: a close-up of his raised hand, the exact shatter pattern on the floor, the way his face had contorted. Each time the images surfaced, the same paralyzing terror rushed through her chest, as vivid as the day it happened. Mai had come to believe she was permanently changed for the worse. She was certain that you could never know who would harm you, and that violence could arrive from anyone, at any moment, without warning. This certainty made ordinary interactions feel fraught. She began scanning every face in her tutoring studio, watching hands and shoulders for signs of aggression, calculating exits the moment she walked into a room. Her work as a tutor, once a quiet anchor, became a landscape of constant monitoring. When students sat at her desk, her breathing would catch; she avoided certain rooms in her own home where objects had been left within reach, and she stopped attending neighborhood gatherings. She felt like a permanent outsider now, watching the world from behind a pane of glass she could not see but could never escape. Months of this relentless alertness accumulated into a profound exhaustion. She had learned that her habits of scanning and withdrawal kept her functional but only at the cost of her marriage and her daily rhythm. Her husband’s gentle questions about her distance felt like threats to her peace, and she found herself isolating in the back corner of the tutoring space, grading papers with her back to the door. What finally brought her to seek help was a Tuesday morning when a student’s dropped pencil box made her slam into the wall, drawing alarmed stares from her colleagues. The sheer volume of her fear had become undeniable. She came to the clinic hoping to understand why her body still braced for attacks that no longer existed, and what frightened her most was that the damage was too deep to ever be undone. She hoped, however faintly, to stop feeling like a permanent outsider in her own life.
